turns.question_text: Imagine you and a friend are putting together a dinner for just the two of you. You've offered to plan and cook, which would take a big chunk of an afternoon, and you asked them to cover the groceries. They tell you they'd like to do it but buying everything feels like too much for them. What do you say back?
turns.answer_text: I'd ask what kind of budget they're comfortable with and offer to chip in on the pricier stuff, or we could just split the receipt. If they still seemed uneasy after that, honestly I can't say whether I'd keep trying to work something out or just drop it and cook with whatever I already have.

turns.question_text: Say a friend and you are planning a meal for two. You volunteer to organise and cook for several hours and ask them to buy the ingredients, but they say they'd like to do it and paying for everything is too much. How do you respond?
turns.answer_text: I'd tell them that's fair and ask what they could afford. Maybe I'd cover the main ingredients and they'd bring dessert and wine. If that still didn't sit right with them, I'd keep adjusting with them until we landed on something we were both fine with. I don't like leaving it unsettled, so I'd stay at it until we had a version we both liked.

turns.question_text: Suppose you're organising a group gift for a coworker, and one of the people you asked to chip in says the amount is too much for them. What would you say to them?
turns.answer_text: I'd tell them no problem and say to give whatever they're comfortable with.

turns.question_text: When you show up at a relaxed meal with people you know and nobody has given you a job, what do you tend to notice first?
turns.answer_text: Who's already in the kitchen, and whether there's something obvious nobody is covering, like drinks or setting out plates.

turns.question_text: A friend is moving and you promised to help sort things, but it's eating into time you'd set aside for yourself, and they'd be fine with adjusting the plan. What matters most as you decide what to do?
turns.answer_text: Mostly that I keep my word without ending up resenting it, so I'd want to be honest with them about my limits.

turns.question_text: Suppose your planner app is simple, works offline, and covers what you need, but it can't share reminders. A newer app adds shared reminders and better search, but it's more complicated and moving everything would take about an hour. What would matter in deciding whether to switch?
turns.answer_text: I'd want to try it out on a few items first and read what other people say about it.

turns.question_text: Imagine your basic needs are covered and you unexpectedly receive a sum equal to about a month of your usual living costs, with no strings attached. What would you most want that money to do for you?
turns.answer_text: I'd sit down and look through the options with my partner before deciding anything.

turns.question_text: You and a friend are planning a meal for just the two of you. You offer to organise and cook it over several hours and ask them to buy the ingredients. They say they'd like to do the meal, but paying for all the ingredients feels like too much. What would you say next?
turns.answer_text: I'd ask them what amount would feel fair to them.

turns.question_text: You're on a bus route you ride all the time, and the driver abruptly turns onto a road that route never uses to reach your stop. How do you read that?
turns.answer_text: I'd look out the window and ask the driver or someone nearby what's going on.

turns.question_text: You promised to help a friend sort belongings for a move, but it's running long and cutting into your own planned time. They're open to changing the arrangement. What would matter most in deciding what to do?
turns.answer_text: I really can't say what would matter most. I've never been in that situation and I don't want to guess.

turns.question_text: With your basics covered, you unexpectedly get extra money equal to roughly one month of your normal expenses, with no repayment or tax attached. What would you most want it to do for you?
turns.answer_text: I'd put it toward a trip to visit my sister, since I haven't seen her in years.

turns.question_text: Your needs are covered and you unexpectedly receive about a month's worth of your ordinary living costs, no obligations attached. What would you most want that money to do for you?
Is there anything about your last answer you'd like to change?
turns.answer_text: Yes, ignore the laptop. I'd actually keep it as a cushion so I could turn down extra shifts.

turns.question_text: Your current planning app is simple, familiar and works offline, but can't share reminders. A new one shares reminders and searches better, but it's more complex and the move would take about an hour. What would matter in deciding whether to switch?
turns.answer_text: I'd stay put. Simplicity and working offline matter most to me, and I wouldn't give those up just to share reminders.

turns.question_text: Picture choosing between your old offline planner and a newer, more complex one that offers shared reminders, with an hour of migration. What would tip the decision for you?
turns.answer_text: I'd switch right away. Shared reminders alone are worth the hour, and the extra complexity doesn't bother me much.

turns.question_text: Say you unexpectedly receive roughly one month of your usual living costs with no repayment strings and your basics are already covered. What would you most want it to do for you?
turns.answer_text: I'd want to look at my accounts and bills before deciding.

turns.question_text: You walk into an informal shared meal with a few people you know, and nobody has asked you to do anything in particular. What usually catches your attention first?
turns.answer_text: I tend to check whether the host looks like they need anything, and then I find where people are talking.
